questions.question: A patient has Strongyloides stercoralis with concurrent filarial co-infection.

parts.text: What is the risk of ivermectin?
Name two ways to handle a patient from a Strongyloides-endemic region who is about to start immunosuppression.

parts_raw.text: a) What is the risk of ivermectin?
b) 2 ways to handle those from an endemic region for Strongy going to start immunosuppression

questions.model_answer: a) In heavy Loa loa co-infection, ivermectin can precipitate a fatal encephalopathy from rapid killing of high-level microfilaremia (a Mazzotti-type reaction); check for Loa loa (blood smear/serology) and consider albendazole pre-treatment before giving ivermectin. b) (1) Screen before immunosuppression with Strongyloides serology (recombinant NIE/SsIR ELISA, near 100% sensitivity) plus stool exams, and treat any positive with ivermectin. (2) If screening is unavailable or high pre-test probability, treat empirically/presumptively with ivermectin, because immunosuppression (especially corticosteroids) can trigger fatal hyperinfection/dissemination in a chronically, lifelong-infected host.
questions.beyond_mandell: The Loa loa/ivermectin encephalopathy risk is from the filariasis literature, not this chapter. Screening/empiric-treatment rationale grounded in the chapter's discussion of chronic infection and immunosuppression-driven hyperinfection.

cohort_answer.text: a) If heavy Loa loa infection, ivermectin can precipitate an encephalopathy (mechanism unknown, believed related to high microfilaremia and rapid killing of worms - Mazzotti reaction); pre-treat with Albendazole. b) Screen with stool and serology (high sens, low specificity, positive with Wuchereria, Brugia, Onchocerca, Mansonella); Treat empirically with Albendazole or apheresis.

questions.question: A patient has strongyloidiasis.

parts.text: Why is there concern about treating with ivermectin if the patient is from a filaria-endemic region (East/West Africa)?

parts_raw.text: a) Why is there a concern to treat with ivermectin if from a filaria endemic region (East/West Africa)?

questions.model_answer: a) The patient may be co-infected with Loa loa. In heavy Loa loa infection (high microfilaremia), ivermectin can precipitate a potentially fatal encephalopathy through rapid microfilarial killing. Screen for Loa loa (daytime blood smear/serology) first; Loa loa itself requires diethylcarbamazine (DEC), and heavy loiasis may need albendazole pre-treatment or apheresis before microfilaricidal therapy.
questions.beyond_mandell: Loa loa co-infection and ivermectin-induced encephalopathy are covered in the filariasis chapter, not this intestinal-nematode chapter; answer per Mandell/CDC filariasis guidance.

cohort_answer.text: If patient has Loa Loa, ivermectin may precipitate encephalopathy (Loa Loa needs to be treated with DEC). Dx with serology or smear. Loa Loa: filarial nematode causing subcutaneous filariasis, vector = chrysops silacea and dimidiata (deerflies, bite during day). Takes ~5 months for larvae to become adult worms. Majority asymptomatic; symptoms - Calabar swellings and eye worm.
